info.title: Spool API
info.description: The REST API of a Spool server: a self-hosted git forge that keeps every repository in object storage. Git smart-HTTP endpoints (clone/fetch/push at /{org}/{repo}.git) speak the standard git wire protocol and are not described here. Every repository is private to the organization that owns it: a request with no credential answers 401 on every repository, changeset, search and profile route, and a credential that may not read a repository gets the same 404 a repository that does not exist gets. The exceptions are the sign-in routes under /v1/auth, the health and metrics probes, the inbound webhook receiver, the runner routes (which take their own credentials) and the signed CDN pack URL. Errors return JSON {"error": "…"} with the matching status. Optimistic-concurrency conflicts return 409 with the current tip.

bearer.description: Token of the form weft_<id>_<secret>. Scopes: org:admin, org:read, repo:read, repo:write. A token acts only in the organization it was minted in: presented anywhere else it has no access, and a repository there answers 404. Repo-bound tokens are restricted to one repository and cannot search.

session.name: stratum_session
session.description: Browser session from POST /v1/auth/login. An alternative to a bearer token for the dashboard; a bearer token wins when both are presented. A session spans every organization its person belongs to, which is why anything that crosses two namespaces — forking, opening a change from a fork — takes one. Routes under /v1/auth use this scheme.

self_hosted_repos.description: Repository names, sorted. Only consulted under `selected`, but returned always so a dashboard switching back still has the list somebody chose.

runners.description: How many live machines are in it.

labels.description: What this machine will match. The server always adds `self-hosted`, the OS and the architecture to whatever custom labels it offered.

ephemeral.description: Registered to run one job and then de-register.

state.description: Derived, never stored: `busy` if a running job points at it, else `online` if it called within the last 60 seconds, else `offline`. There is no status column for a crashed process to leave lying.

job.description: What it is running right now, or null.

job_id.description: The workflow job's row id — what a link into the run needs.

repo.description: The repository's name — not its id. A run is addressed by `owner/repo`, so this is what a link to the build needs.

stored_bytes.description: What this repository holds in the object store, in bytes, as of the last push or storage sweep. Shown on the repository page; nothing is metered or capped by it.

origin_url.description: Origin identity for a mirror — a fetchable URL for the generic provider, or "owner/name" for the GitHub App provider. Null for native repos.

clone_url.description: HTTPS git remote for this repo.

ssh_clone_url.description: SSH git remote (ssh://git@host:port/org/repo.git), or null when the deployment has no SSH front door configured.

origin_provider.description: Origin integration backing a mirror; null for native repos.

origin_installation.description: GitHub App installation id used to mint fetch credentials for this mirror; null unless origin_provider is "github".

homepage.description: The project's own address on the web, shown in the repository's About panel. Always an absolute http:// or https:// URL, or null — a scheme-less "example.com" is refused rather than repaired, because prepending a scheme is wrong in exactly the case that matters: a relative URL resolving against this host, wearing the project's name. Empty and whitespace-only are stored as null, so "no homepage" has one encoding rather than two.

fork_count.description: Repositories forked directly from this one that the caller may read. The count a caller may see, not a stored total — forks live in other namespaces, and publishing the stored number would say how many exist that the caller cannot see.

watcher_count.description: People subscribed to everything that happens here. Counts only the "all" watch level: the default subscription is stored as no row at all, so counting the table would rise when somebody chose to be left alone. On this view rather than on .../watch — that endpoint is the caller's own setting, so a masthead reading it would have a number for some readers and not others.

fork_state.description: Fork preparation state; absent on a repository that is not a fork. A fork's row exists immediately and its storage pointers a moment later, which is why forking answers 202.

org.description: The namespace this repository is in, by name. The row carries org_id, which is no use to a client: after forking into 'wherever I belong', the answer to 'where did it go' is a name.

commits.description: How many commits are reachable from the default branch's tip — every parent of every commit, as GitHub counts — as of the last time the compaction job that follows every write counted them. Null until it has. Stored rather than computed on the request: a repository page must not walk history to print a number.

commits_tip.description: The commit `commits` was counted from. A client that knows the current tip compares the two and shows the number only while they agree, rather than printing a count that is a push behind as though it were current.

commits_exact.description: False when the walk stopped at STRATUM_COMMIT_COUNT_CAP (default 100000) with history still to go; the true number is then at least `commits`. True when there is no count yet, so a client has one flag to read.

fork_parent.description: owner/name of what this was forked from, when the viewer may see it. Null covers three different facts on purpose: not a fork, upstream deleted and this promoted, or an upstream this viewer may not see — which is why it cannot be derived client-side from an id.

viewer_admin.description: Whether the caller may administer this repository — default branch, branch protections, access. Answered by the server because the two authorities differ: patch and the protections routes accept a per-repo admin grant, while the access listing requires org-wide admin, so a client inferring one from the other hides the settings surface from somebody entitled to it.

viewer_member.description: Whether the caller holds a role on this repository — an organization membership or a per-repo grant. Every caller who can read the repository at all has one, so this is true for every reader; it is kept because the Insights tab and older clients read it. Weaker than `viewer_write`: the `viewer` role is a member who may not push.

viewer_write.description: Whether the caller may push here, and so whether they may open a change whose commits are already in this repository. Distinct from viewer_admin: a member writes without administering, and a `viewer` or a contributor proposing from a fork reads without either. Answered by the server because it is the scope POST /changes actually checks before refusing a change that names no source — a client guessing it either hides the form from somebody who may use it, or offers one to a reader and refuses them after they have filled it in.

push.description: For a mirror: whether a push to it is forwarded to its origin, and if not, why. null for a native repository. `forwarding` is the answer; `blocked` is the sentence a push would be refused with; `needs_permission` with `approve_url` is an installation that predates `Contents: write`.

expected_parent.description: Optimistic concurrency: the branch must currently point here (null = branch must not exist; omitted = commit on the current tip).

context.description: Free-form audit blob recorded immutably with the commit.

org.description: Namespace name — a repo name alone is ambiguous across namespaces.

get.summary: Whether this organization admits self-hosted runners, and for which repositories (org:read)
get.description: Every workflow job on this server runs on a runner the organization registered, so this one switch decides where workflows run at all: `all` (the default) admits every repository, `selected` only those in `self_hosted_repos`, and `disabled` none. A repository the policy does not admit has its runs failed at trigger time with "self-hosted runners are not allowed for this repository (organisation policy)".

200.description: The policy as it stands

patch.description: Either key or both; an absent key is left alone. `self_hosted_repos` is a list of repository names and is replaced wholesale — `[]` clears it. Audited as `runner_policy.updated`. A refusal here is a refusal at trigger time rather than a job queued forever: a push to a repository the policy does not admit becomes a failed run reading "self-hosted runners are not allowed for this repository (organisation policy)".

self_hosted_repos.description: Repository names in this organisation. A name that is not there is a 422 rather than a silent drop: a group that quietly admits four of the five somebody listed is a build that does not run and a settings page that says it should.

200.description: The policy as it now stands

404.description: No such organisation, or the caller is not an admin of it

422.description: A value outside the enumeration, or a repository name that is not there

get.summary: Runner groups in this organisation (org:read)
get.description: A group is the unit a repository is admitted by, and every machine is in exactly one. Every organisation has a `default` group, created lazily the first time anything needs one — so this never answers an empty list.

200.description: { groups: […] }

409.description: A group of that name already exists

patch.description: Any subset; an absent key is left alone, and `repos` is replaced wholesale. The default group's name is fixed (422): it is the name printed in every registration command ever handed out, and renaming it would silently point those at nothing. Audited as `runner_group.updated`.

repos.description: Repository names in this organisation. A name that is not there is a 422 rather than a silent drop: a group that quietly admits four of the five somebody listed is a build that does not run and a settings page that says it should.

200.description: The group as it now stands

404.description: No such group in this organisation

409.description: Another group already has that name

422.description: An invalid value, or an attempt to rename the default group

delete.summary: Delete a runner group (org:admin)
delete.description: Its machines move to the default group rather than being removed: an operator tidying their groups has not asked to take thirty machines offline, and a runner whose group vanished would authenticate and then never be routed anything — the least debuggable failure this feature has. Any outstanding registration token for the group goes with it. The default group cannot be deleted. Audited as `runner_group.deleted`.

204.description: Deleted; its machines are now in the default group

404.description: No such group in this organisation

get.summary: The machines this organisation has registered (org:read)
get.description: Live machines only. A removed one is tombstoned rather than deleted — a job row names the machine that ran it, and a reader looking at last week's build should still be told which — but it is gone from here.

200.description: { runners: […] }

post.summary: Mint a single-use registration token (org:admin)
post.description: One hour, one machine. Hashed at rest like every other bearer secret here, because it travels through a shell history and a terminal scrollback on its way to the machine. `command` is the whole `weft-runner register` line spelled out, with the server's own public URL (STRATUM_PUBLIC_URL) — the alternative is a reader assembling it from three fields and getting `--url` wrong, which fails at registration with a network error that says nothing about which part was wrong. Audited as `runner.registration_token.created`.

group.description: The group the machine will join.

201.description: The only time the token exists

404.description: No such organisation, or the caller is not an admin of it

delete.summary: Remove a machine (org:admin)
delete.description: Its credential is dead from the next call it makes — which is the whole revocation mechanism, since nothing is listening on the operator's network to be told. A job running on it is failed, with the error "runner removed while the job was running", and deliberately not handed to the next machine in the group: an operator who removes a runner has decided the machine should stop, and a silent re-run somewhere else is the opposite of what they asked for. Audited as `runner.removed`.

404.description: No such machine in this organisation

post.summary: Exchange a registration token for the machine's own credential
post.description: Not a route a person calls, and not a session or an API token: the bearer here is the one-hour `weftg_…` secret from the registration-token route, and it names the organisation and the group, so the machine never has to assert either. Every way the token can be wrong — malformed, unknown, already spent, expired — is the same 401, so it cannot be used to learn which organisations exist. Registering under a name that is already live replaces that machine, tombstoning the old row in the same transaction: that is how a credential is rotated, and how a reimaged machine comes back without somebody having to remove it by hand first. Audited as `runner.registered`.

name.description: Letters, digits, dot, dash, underscore; at most 64. Defaults to the hostname on the runner side.

labels.description: Custom labels only. `self-hosted`, the OS and the architecture are added by the server, so a job's `runs-on` can rely on them being there.

ephemeral.description: Run one job, then de-register. The autoscaling shape.

201.description: The only time the credential exists

credential.description: `weftr_…`. Hashed at rest and never recoverable; re-register to get another.

401.description: The registration token is unknown, already used or expired

422.description: A name, label, OS or architecture outside what is allowed

post.summary: Ask for work, and wait a while for some
post.description: The bearer is the machine's own `weftr_…` credential. A long poll: the server holds the request open for `STRATUM_RUNNER_CLAIM_WAIT_MS` (20 s by default), re-running its claim every 500 ms, and answers 204 if nothing came. That is the whole scaling story — asking every second is one query per machine per second forever, almost all of it answering "nothing"; asking every thirty is half a minute of latency on every build. Set the client's HTTP timeout longer than the server's wait, so a 204 arrives as a 204 rather than as a client-side timeout. Every call touches `last_seen_at`, which is what the runner list's `online` reading is made of. A job is routed to this machine only if its `runs-on` labels are a subset of the machine's, the machine's group admits the repository, and the organisation's policy admits self-hosted runners for it — three different people's decisions, all re-read here and not only at trigger time, because a job can sit in the queue across a settings change. On 200 the machine then makes the five per-job calls under /v1/runner/jobs/{id}, with the `token` from here.

200.description: A job was assigned

token.description: The per-job, per-attempt credential for the five runner calls: `repo:read` on one repository, revoked the moment the verdict lands.

runner_url.description: The base URL to report on — the address this machine already reached, not the public one. They are the same behind a CDN and differ on a private network.

204.description: Nothing to run after the wait. Ask again.

401.description: This credential is unknown, or the machine has been removed. The runner prints that it has been removed and exits: there is no way back without registering.

409.description: { error: "busy" } — this machine already holds a running job. A runner runs one job at a time, and a second would be work nobody ever reports on.

get.summary: A person's profile
get.description: Display name, bio, location, company, pronouns, account kind (human or agent) and links: the directory entry for a person on this server. Needs a signed-in caller — a session or a personal token; with none the answer is 401. It never carries an email address and never lists repositories. A disabled account has no profile and answers 404; its namespace stays claimed so nobody can move in behind them.

200.description: { handle, name, display_name, bio, location, company, pronouns, kind, profile_repo, created_at, links: [{ label, url }] }

404.description: No such handle, or the account is disabled

patch.description: Every field is optional: an absent key leaves it alone, an explicit null clears it. `links` replaces the whole list (at most 5) and every url must be http or https — a profile link is rendered as an anchor on a page other people load, so `javascript:` and `data:` are refused. Nobody may patch anybody else's profile.

200.description: The profile as it now reads

400.description: A field is over its cap, holds a control character, or a link is not http(s)

403.description: This is somebody else's account

404.description: No such handle

get.summary: The addresses on your own account, proved or not
get.description: Readable only by the account itself, never by another. This is the authorship-linkage surface — the set that decides which commits count as this person's work — so showing it to anybody else would hand an impersonator the exact string to put in `git config user.email`, and a spammer a mailbox.

200.description: { emails: [{ address, verified_at, private, primary, created_at }] }

403.description: This is somebody else's account

404.description: No such handle

post.summary: Claim an address and mail it a confirmation link
post.description: Body: { email }. The claim is worth nothing on its own: the row lands unproved, and only a verified address may ever carry authorship. The link goes to the mailbox and never into the response — a claim confirmed over the API would prove nothing. It is bound both to the address and to this account, so it cannot be spent against a different mailbox or from a different session. At most 10 addresses per account.

400.description: Not an address, or the account is at its address limit

403.description: This is somebody else's account

409.description: Already yours, or already in use. Which account holds it is never disclosed.

post.summary: Spend a confirmation link and mark that one address proved
post.description: Body: { token }. Every wrong shape — malformed, unknown, expired, already spent, or issued to another account — answers the same 404, so a link cannot be used to ask which addresses are registered here.

200.description: { address, verified: true }

403.description: This is somebody else's account

404.description: This confirmation link is not valid any more

delete.summary: Drop an address from your account
delete.description: The address you sign in with is refused — an account with no reachable address is one nobody can recover — and so is an address that is not yours, with the same answer.

403.description: This is somebody else's account

404.description: No such address on this account, or it is the address you sign in with

get.summary: An organization's profile
get.description: Display name, description, location, website and contact address. Needs a signed-in caller; with none the answer is 401. An org that has never been edited reads exactly like one whose fields were cleared — there is no second “no profile yet” state for a page to handle.

200.description: { org, display_name, description, location, website, contact_email }

404.description: No such org

patch.description: Optional fields; an explicit null clears one. `website` must be http or https and `contact_email` must be an address, for the same reason the personal profile holds them to it: both are rendered on a page other people load.

200.description: The profile as it now reads

400.description: A field is over its cap, the website is not http(s), or the contact address is not an address

403.description: Needs org:admin

404.description: No such org, or the caller is not a member

post.summary: Sign in with email and password; sets an HttpOnly session cookie. Every failure — unknown address, wrong password, disabled account — answers 401 identically.

200.description: { id, email, name, created_at, orgs: [{ id, name, role }] }

post.summary: End this session and clear the cookie. Answers 204 even without a valid session — a stale cookie still has to go.

get.summary: The signed-in person and the orgs they can reach (session cookie)

200.description: { id, email, name, created_at, orgs: [{ id, name, role }] }

post.summary: Redeem an invitation link, creating the account if this is a new person, and sign in. Single use.

201.description: { id, email, name, created_at, orgs: [...] } and a session cookie

400.description: invite is unknown, expired, already used, or the name/password is unusable

post.summary: What an invitation is for, before committing to it: the namespace, the role and the address it was sent to. No credentials — the token in the body is the credential.

200.description: { org, role, email, expires_at }

404.description: every dead link answers identically — malformed, unknown, expired, already accepted or a wrong secret — so a link cannot be used to probe which invitations exist

post.summary: Create an account and its personal namespace, and mail a confirmation link. The handle is checked first and its refusals are plain — namespace names are unique on the server and appear in every clone URL, so "that one is taken" gives nothing away. Everything after that answers identically whether or not the address is already registered.

202.description: { status, detail } — always this, whether a message was sent, the address already has an account (its owner is mailed a note saying nothing was created), or the rate limit was hit

400.description: invalid handle, address, name, or a password under 12 characters

409.description: that handle is taken or reserved

post.summary: Redeem a confirmation link and sign in. Single-use; sets the session cookie.

200.description: the account, as /v1/auth/me returns it

404.description: malformed, unknown, spent, expired, or a reset token presented here

get.summary: Begin signing in with GitHub. Answers a 303 to GitHub's authorization screen and parks a single-use anti-CSRF state in an HttpOnly `weft_ghauth` cookie; the callback refuses unless the `state` it is handed matches that cookie, which is what proves the browser finishing the flow is the one that started it. Takes no credentials — the caller is by definition not signed in yet. A deployment whose App has no OAuth client configured redirects to the dashboard with `github=unavailable` rather than leaving for a URL that cannot work.

303.description: redirect to GitHub's authorization screen, or to the dashboard with `github=unavailable`

get.summary: GitHub sends a browser here after the authorization screen. The `state` must match the `weft_ghauth` cookie this browser was given, and the `code` is exchanged for the person's token to read `GET /user` and `GET /user/emails`. An account is resolved in three steps: the linked identity, keyed on GitHub's numeric user id so a renamed login still lands on it; then an account whose sign-in address matches one GitHub reports **primary and verified**; then a new account, created with no password and with its address already proved, so it may create immediately without a confirmation mail. Only the `verified` flag is trusted — an unproved primary answers `noemail` and makes nothing. Answers a redirect into the dashboard either way, carrying `github=ok|new|denied|expired|noemail|emailtaken|disabled|unavailable|error`; `ok` and `new` also set the session cookie, and `new` is the only one with onboarding left to do.

parameters.name: code
parameters.description: GitHub's user-authorization code, spent on the first exchange. Absent is `github=expired`.

parameters.name: state
parameters.description: Must equal the `weft_ghauth` cookie, and neither may be empty. Absent, empty or mismatched is `github=expired` — one answer for all of them, so a callback cannot be used to probe.

parameters.name: error
parameters.description: GitHub's own refusal, `access_denied` when the person pressed Cancel. Reported as `github=denied`, which is a choice rather than a failure.

303.description: redirect to the dashboard with the outcome in `github`

post.summary: Send another confirmation link. Answers identically for a live account, an already-confirmed one, an unknown address and a malformed one.
Mail a password-reset link. Same uniform answer as resend-verification. A disabled account gets no link — recovering one an operator switched off would undo the switching off.

Redeem a reset link, set a new password, and sign in. Ends every other session on the account. Password strength is checked before the link is spent, so a typo costs a retry rather than another trip through the inbox.

400.description: the new password is under 12 characters

404.description: malformed, unknown, spent, expired, or a verification token presented here

delete.summary: Delete a repo (instant tombstone; storage swept by GC)
delete.description: The row is tombstoned at once and the storage is swept by GC later. Side effects that are not deferred: forks are detached and survive, and CI stops — every run still going is cancelled with "the repository was deleted", its jobs and their mirrored check runs settle as `cancelled`, running jobs have their job tokens revoked, so their runners learn to stop on their next call, and queued jobs are never handed out. Without that last part a deleted repository goes on occupying the organization's runners until each job's timeout expires.

patch.summary: Edit a repo's description, homepage, default branch, or the installation a mirror pushes through
patch.description: One handler, four fields, two different authorities. `description` absent leaves it alone; `null` or "" clears it, and editing it needs only repo:write. `homepage` behaves identically and carries the same authority, with one extra rule: it must be an absolute http:// or https:// URL. It is rendered as an anchor on a page other people load, so `javascript:` and `data:` are refused for the same reason profile links are — and a scheme-less "example.com" is refused rather than repaired, since prepending one is wrong exactly when it produces a relative URL resolving against this host. There is no visibility to change: `"public": true` is a 400, and `false` is accepted and changes nothing. `default_branch` requires org:admin and the branch must already exist; a mirror's default branch follows its origin and cannot be set here. `installation_id` attaches the GitHub App installation a mirror forwards pushes through — org:admin, GitHub mirrors only, and the organization must have connected it (an id it never earned is a 404, exactly as at creation).

homepage.description: Absolute http:// or https:// URL, or null/"" to clear. Absent leaves it alone.

public.description: Accepted only as false; `true` is a 400. Every repository is private to its organization.

installation_id.description: A GitHub App installation this organization has connected; the mirror forwards pushes through it from then on.

200.description: The repo as it now is

post.summary: Apply a reviewer's suggestion blocks as one new patchset
post.description: A suggestion is a fenced `suggestion` block inside a review comment's body — there is no suggestion field and no suggestion column; it is parsed where it is read, so an imported or mirrored comment carries one exactly as a comment written here does. The block replaces the lines its comment is anchored to (`path` plus `line`/`line_end`, `side: new`); an **empty** block means delete those lines, which is distinct from a comment carrying no block at all. Every named comment is applied in **one** commit on top of the latest patchset and registered through the same path a push takes, so a reviewer's five remarks become one revision, one CI run and one notification rather than five. Nothing is rewritten: the new commit's parent is the patchset the reviewer read, which is what makes this clean under fast-forward-only landing. The commit message is the latest patchset's, so the `Change-Id` trailer keeps it a patchset of the same change — a change whose commit carries no trailer is refused, because a commit built from it would open a new change instead.

Approval is **per tip**: a new patchset from the fork is blocked again, like GitHub's "Approve and run". The blocked placeholder run and its check row are replaced by the real run for the same commit and file.

post.summary: Enqueue the change for landing (fast-forward promotion by the land worker)
post.description: The precheck asks `land_gate`, not "is any check currently failing". The old question let two things through that a green tick then misrepresented: a change with no checks at all, and one whose checks had not started. A required check that has **not reported** is now a wait rather than an acceptance — and a wait, not a refusal, because ejecting somebody the moment they press Land before CI has started is the polling a land queue exists to abolish. The change is accepted, held in the queue, and lands unattended when the check reports green; a required check that never reports at all is ejected by the wait budget with a message naming it. A required check that has failed, or a non-required one that has, refuses here in words rather than being accepted and ejected seconds later.

202.description: { queued, job, change, gate, waiting_on } — `gate` is "ready" or "waiting", and `waiting_on` names the required checks still to report. The lander re-verifies sufficiency, the gate and fast-forward at claim time, so a 202 is a promise to try rather than a promise to land.

The other three refusals — not open, already landing, not landable — are not gate decisions and carry `error` alone: emitting `gate` for them would say the gate had an opinion when it was never consulted. Read `reason ?? error`.

post.description: Pre-flight first, and it writes nothing: every member must be `open`, its sufficiency verdict at the latest patchset green, its required checks **passing** — a check that has not reported is a refusal here where a single change would be held, because the plan below is made against the trunks as they stand now — and its patchset a fast-forward of its target. The changeset's composed CI is part of that gate too: a composed check failing, cancelled or skipped is a refusal, and one still queued or running is a `waiting` refusal here, the same as a member's own. Landing does not cancel composed runs. Then the commit point: one landing record with the full plan, and the changeset turns `landing` in the same transaction. From that row on the landing *will* finish, on this node or any other: members are CASed in landing order one manifest at a time; a member whose trunk moved in the window fails the landing, and every member already landed is put back with a **revert commit** on top of the landed one — never a rewind. `GET …/changesets/{changeset}` carries the landing's progress member by member until the changeset is `landed` or `failed`. A landed member is `landed` with `land_verdict` "landed with changeset {key}"; a reverted one is `open` again with a verdict naming the revert and what failed, and needs a new patchset to land again; a member that never got its turn is `open` with an `ejected:` verdict.

A member that is not a fast-forward of its trunk is `repo/change: not fast-forward from {tip}`, with `gate` "blocked".

post.description: Body { key, title?, body? }. In every repository a member of this changeset landed in, makes one commit on a new `revert/{key}` branch off the target branch **as it is now** that puts back every path the member changed — the deleted file returns, the rewritten one is its old self at its old mode, the added ones are gone — and leaves every other path alone, so work landed since is kept. Each commit is registered as a change on the member's target exactly as a push would be (pinned, CI triggered, owners notified), and the changes are composed into changeset `key` with this changeset's edges **reversed**: what landed after its dependency is undone before it. Nothing about this changeset moves, and no trunk moves: the new changeset is reviewed under the same OWNERS and landed with `POST …/land` like any other. Only members recorded as landed are reverted — every member of a `landed` changeset, and of a `failed` one the members the unwind left landed (`GET …/changesets/{changeset}` shows them `done` with a `not reverted` note). Every member is checked before any branch is written, and any one refusal refuses the whole call: a path somebody has changed on trunk since the landing, a target branch that is gone, a `revert/{key}` branch already there, a member whose repository has been deleted. Title defaults to `Revert "{title}"`, body to `Reverts changeset {key}.`.

When a member cannot be reverted cleanly, `error` names the first in landing order — `{repo}/{change}: {ref} has changed since it landed at {paths}`, `{repo}/{change}: {ref} no longer exists`, `{repo}/{change}: revert/{key} already exists` — and `conflicts` lists every such member as { repo, change, why, changed?: [path], no_branch?, branch_exists? }. Which organization: the single-use `state` minted by `POST /v1/orgs/{org}/github/install`; without one (GitHub sends none after an edit, and an install begun on GitHub or from the Marketplace never had one) the signed-in person's own single pending connect stands in; otherwise the installation, already proved theirs, is parked and the browser is sent to `connect=claim` with a claim cookie, and `POST /v1/orgs/{org}/github/install/claim` binds it after sign-in. Answers a redirect back into the dashboard either way, carrying `connect=ok|claim|notyours|missing|expired|taken|error` — every dead state is `expired`, so a callback cannot be used to learn which flows exist.

get.summary: What the repository is, beside what is in it: the language mix by bytes, the detected licence, the community files (CONTRIBUTING / CODE_OF_CONDUCT / SECURITY) found at the root or in `.github/`, the path of the README, and the topics. Everything but the topics is derived from the tree at the default branch — no new git plumbing and nothing stored. Readable by anyone who may read the repository; 401 with no credential, and masked exactly as the code is for anyone who may not. `license.spdx` is null with `recognised: false` when the file is there but the fingerprint table is not certain what it is — a wrong licence is materially worse than no licence, so it never guesses. get.summary: This repository's workflow runs, newest first, each with its jobs
get.description: What `.weft/` actually ran — as opposed to `/workflows`, which is what it *would* run. Run JSON is `{ id, file, name, commit_sha, ref_name, event, change_key, state, error, blocked_reason, created_at, updated_at, completed_at, changeset, composition, jobs: [...] }`; `event` is `push`, `change` or `changeset`, and on a `changeset` run `changeset` is `{ key }` and `composition` is the hex composition it was started for — both null otherwise; `state` is one of running, passed, failed, cancelled, blocked — a run that exists, is not running and has no verdict: a fork's change waiting for a maintainer to let it run. The sentence is in `error` and the machine-readable reason is in `blocked_reason` — `fork`, and null unless the run is blocked. Branch on `blocked_reason`, never on the words in `error`: a `fork` run is started by `POST …/changes/{change}/workflows/approve`, and the sentences are written for a person and get rewritten. The run's mirrored check row is `queued` rather than failing, because nothing is wrong with the commit. Job JSON is `{ id, job_id, key, matrix, state, attempts, error, detail_url, log_chunks, pool, labels, runner, started_at, completed_at }`; `pool` is always `self_hosted` (kept for clients written for the hosted edition), `labels` is what the job's `runs-on` asked for, and `runner` is `{ id, name }` once a runner has claimed it, null before; `key` is the expanded cell name and `matrix` is an object, already parsed. The complete log once the job has uploaded it, and the chunks produced so far while it is still running — the two are the same bytes read at different times, so no caller has to know which half of a job's life it is looking at. get.summary: A job's build log as it arrives (server-sent events)
get.description: `text/event-stream`. Emits `event: chunk` carrying `{ "text": ... }` for each new log chunk, in order, `event: queued` once for a job that has not started, and `event: done` carrying `{ "state": ... }` when the job leaves running/queued, after which the stream closes. The chunk is JSON rather than the raw bytes because an SSE `data:` field cannot carry a newline — the wire format splits a multi-line payload across several `data:` lines and loses the payload's trailing one, which would run the last line of each chunk into the first line of the next. Held open for at most six hours. The feed reads the same stored chunk objects the plain log route does rather than an in-memory fan-out from the runner: on a server of several nodes, the node a runner posts to is not the node a reader is connected to, and an in-process channel would show the log to whoever happened to land on the right one and a spinner to everybody else.

get.summary: Everything a runner needs to check out and execute one job
get.description: Called by `weft-runner`; not a route a person calls. The credential is a **job token**: minted for one attempt of one job, `repo:read` on one repository, with an expiry, and recorded on the job row. A token that is valid for the repository but was not minted for this job is 403 — otherwise one build could report another's verdict.
